text.p: The copper market ended a dramatic year with a whimper on Tuesday, with this key metal and most others little traded due to the New Year holidays. The LME is closed on Tuesday afternoon and Wednesday for the New Year holiday and reopens on Thursday morning. The January options declaration, which would normally takes place on Wednesday, will now be on Thursday instead.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau Index ended 1.41 points higher at 239.61 on Tuesday.

Benchmark three month copper futures on the London Metal Exchange (LME) ending a quiet morning session at $2,127 a tonne from $2,129 on Monday. "It's been pretty deadly today," said one trader. Prices held a tight range all morning, barely moving on a stock rise of 3,950 tonnes which was in line with expectations. Slow trading conditions during the last few days of 1996 were a far cry from chaotic activity earlier in the year. Prices collapsed to a 2-1/2 year low of $1,745 in June from the year's high of $2,715 just over a month earlier as Japan's Sumitomo Corp uncovered billions of dollars of losses. Cash ended the day at around $92 above three month values.

Aluminium finished the morning kerb on Tuesday at $1,546 from $1,551 on Monday. A stock rise of 5,475 tonnes weighed on values, traders said. Prices finished the year well down on the 1996 peak of $1,700 hit on the first day of the year but even further away from the low reached in October of $1,305.

Lead prices eased, ending Tuesday at $700 from $705 after stocks fell 25 tonnes. Supply shortages and low stocks helped lift prices to a high of $861 in May, but easing tightness caused values to slump to a nadir of $666 in December.

Nickel recovered from Monday's fresh 2-1/4 year low of $6,365 on light short-covering and book-squaring. Three month futures ended the kerb $100 higher at $6,465 after stocks fell 648 tonnes despite expectations of a rise. Prices ended 1996 27 percent below the year's high of $8,850 hit in February.
A 6,500-tonne stock drawdown on Tuesday failed to boost zinc, which finished the day weaker at $1,060 from $1,068. Prices traded in a $997-$1,123 range in 1996.
Tin gained $80 to finish the day at $5,840 after stocks fell 130 tonnes. The highs and lows were $5,680 and $6,650 respectively in 1996.
Aluminium alloy finished last indicated at $1,400 from $1,392/95 on Monday. Stocks rose 560 tonnes. The market traded between $1,190 and $1,495 in 1996.

NYMEX heating oil ended 1996 Tuesday with a sizzling rally on a short squeeze in the expiring January contract that sent crude and gasoline to a strong year-end finish as well. January heating oil settled 2.27 cents higher at 72.84 cents a gallon and January gasoline settled 1.06 cents a gallon up at 70.67 cents ahead of the refined product prompt month expiry. February crude ended 55 cents up at $25.92 a barrel after making a contract high of $25.97. "It's the tail wagging the dog," said a New York dealer, explaining crude prices tracked the heating oil rally. But, traders noted volume was thin in a session shortened to 1300 EST due to the New Year holiday.

CBOT wheat futures closed mostly lower with nearby contracts under pressure from late commission house selling, pit traders said. O'Connor and Co sold 700,000 bushels of March near the close, pit sources said. In other late trade, locals were noted short covering and Cargill Inc bought 300 lots of July, traders said. Traders said selling was tied to ideas farmer sales would pick up after the first of the year. Many farmers had been holding onto grain to defer tax payments until next year and were expected to sell in January. New York precious metals futures ended mostly lower Tuesday, except for palladium which closed sharply higher, but volumes were light and activity was driven by year-end book squaring, traders said. COMEX and NYMEX will close Wednesday for the New Year holiday. "Gold didn't do much, but after yesterday's weakness in silver, more stops were triggered below the $4.80 level (basis March)," North American Equity Services floor trader John Geraghty said. "Palladium jumped on some fund buying, but volumes were light across the board," he said. CSCE world sugar futures closed an abbreviated session barely higher, but gains were enough to lift the most-active March contract through key psychological resistance at 11.00 cents. Fund short-covering carried the contract to a high of 11.02 during the session, where steady trade scale-up selling limited gains, dealers said. Local traders were mixed in their activity. One floor source cited sell stops above 11.05 in March and then over 11.10. The March contract closed at 11.00, up 0.01, while the back months settled 0.01 higher to down 0.02.
